Statement  
     Details of Pilot Scheme for Opening of Franchised Outlets in Specified  
Urban Areas  
1. For providing increased access to postal counter services, Franchising Scheme 
was launched with effect from 1.2.2007 in 88 identi fied urban locations on 
pilot basis. 
2. Basic features of the urban franchise model 
2.1 Only counter services have been franchised, whi le delivery and 
transmission will be continued through the Departme nt. Linking 
arrangements for the franchised outlets will be pro vided by the 
franchisee. 
77 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2007] 
2.2 The franchisee will provide service across the counter for a 
minimum defined time schedule with flexibility to w ork round the 
clock. 
2.3 Products and services offered:  
(a) Sale of stamps and stationery. 
(b) Booking registered articles, speed post articles, money orders (on 
EDBO model), e-post, etc. (no bulk booking to be ta ken up in 
franchised outlets). 
(c) Functioning as an agent of PLI and provide related after sales service, 
including collection of premia (subject to fulfillment of criteria for 
PLI agents). 
(d) Marketing products for which the Department has a corporate agency 
or tie-up and provide related follow up services (subject, to agreement 
which the other organization involved). 
(e) Providing retail and bill/tax/fine collection/payment services of the 
Department (subject to agreement with the other org anizations 
involved). 
(f) Facilitating the provision of e-governance and citizen centric 
services (subject to agreement with the other organ izations 
involved). 
(g) Any other service introduced by the Department in future through its 
outlets which is considered amenable to the franchisee model (subject 
to agreement with the other organizations involved. 
The model has adequate flexibility built in to allow a range of services to be 
extended through the outlets according to the need/demand, and to increase the 
range when found necessary. Thus, the range of counter services that can be 
offered through different outlets can vary, keeping in view the location and its 
capacity to generate revenues. 
2.4 Implementation Strategy:  
In the initial phase and for the present, the urban  franchise model has been 
implemented only in fast developing areas of urban growth like metros and 
their satellite towns, as also such urban areas where there is a justification for 
post offices on the distance and population norms b ut there is difficulty in 
providing the same through redeployment. The 
78 

[10 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
further extension of the scheme can be taken up after the results available from 
experience of the initial phase say after six months of initial launch. 
2.5 Viability:—  
The viability of each franchise only requires to be assessed by the concerned field 
unit so as to ensure adequate returns to the franchisee. The expected minimum revenue 
would depend on the range of services, particular location, potential revenue, the 
investments that the franchisee is willing to make, the cost likely to be incurred by the 
Department in providing support facilities, etc. 
2.6 Criteria for Selection:— 
Applicants for franchises would need to submit an application in a prescribed 
proforma. The selected franchisee will sign a Memorandum of Agreement with the 
Department. Criteria for selection have been fixed considering the need to select persons 
with the capacity to manage and market a range of products, along with a sense of the 
community needs and public aspects of the job, and willingness to accept technological 
options. The criteria are as below: 
(i) Only individuals are eligible for appointment and not any organization 
which he/she may be serving/representing. 
(ii) Age: Above 18 years. No upper age limit. 
(iii) Educational qualification: 10+2 standard of 12th class pass of a recognized 
University or Board of School Education or Board of Secondary Education. 
(iv) Preference: 
(a) Postal pensioners 
(b) Those able to provide computer facilities 
(v) Premises: Proper appropriately located and accessible premises, properly 
maintained with suitable display of approved signages. 
(vi) Applicant should be willing to make the necessary investments for the 
conduct of the business and be able to provide a si mple business plan 
comprising details of how the premises will be . run, what the opening hours 
would be, investments proposed, market conditions, proposals for 
marketing products, awareness of customer base, role in local community, 
budget, 
79 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2007] 
finances, etc. Two references from respectable persons of the locality 
where the franchise is proposed to be located would  also be 
required to establish the character and antecedents of the applicant. 
(vii) A business plan would be prepared taking into  account the 
anticipated minimum level of business/revenue worke d out by the 
Devisional Head for the specific franchise. 
(viii) Security Deposit: The security deposit to be  provided by the 
franchisee would be based on the maximum possible l evel of 
financial transactions likely be undertaken by the franchisee in a day. 
The minimum security deposit would be Rs. 10,000 in the shape of a 
performance bank guarantee. 
(ix) Selection: Would be made by a committee comprising the Heads of the 
concerned Division and a neighbouring Division, based on a report 
from the Assistant Superintendent/Sub Divisional In spector 
(Posts).

Reduction in roaming charges 
3831. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether a proposal from the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India is under 
consideration of Government with regard to reduction in roaming charges; 
(b) whether the Cellular Operators Association of India is resisting this move 
to reduce roaming tariffs; and 
(c) whether the COAI has contended that telecom tariffs  in India are 
among the lowest in the world and further attempts to regulate roaming tariff 
would force them to revise upward the regular tariff? 
81 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS AND 
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) to (c) The roaming 
charges levied by different operators have to be within the ceiling tariff prescribed by the 
Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI). TRAI, after due consultation process with 
all the stakeholders found justifiable grounds for a review of the tariff structure applicable 
for roaming services that had been fixed five years back. 
The Cellular Operators Association of India (COAI) had submitted that the customer 
tariffs are already lowest in the world and consistently coming down and thus, roaming tariffs 
should also be left to market forces. 
Based on in-depth analysis of various elements of cost, data on costs, views of 
stakeholders, the prevailing tariff for calls originated in home networks and other 
relevant factors, TRAI has prescribed a composite ceiling charges for regional/national 
roaming effective from 15th February, 2007. The Cellular Operators have already revised 
roaming tariff accordingly.

Research In Open Software 
3855. SHRI SITARAM YECHURY: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are planning to fund the researc h in Open 
Software or Free Software; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) The Government is promoting research in Free/Open Source Software area by 
supporting various institutions to foster research and development in this area. 
1. Under Indian Language Computing Initiative, National Roll Out project is 
being implemented by Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (CDAC). 
Under this project, the open source softwares such as Office suite, Browser,

these softwares for balance 12 Constitutionally rec ognized languages is

Linux desktop operating system (Bharat Operating Sy stem Solutions-BOSS) 
supporting Indian Language.

applications based on open source and open standard s like 
"Computerization of Police station", "Below Poverty  Line Database", 
"District Suite" etc. Also, specialized application  Collab CAD in the area 
of Computer Aided Design and Manufacture, based on Free/Open Source

organizations in the country. NIC has also started an Open Technology

Statement-I 
Salient features of the guidelines for the districts component of the Backward 
Regions Grant Fund (BRGF)  
t The Backward Regions Grant Fund is designed to redr ess regional 
imbalances in development. The fund will provide fi nancial resources for 
supplementing and converging existing developmental inflows into identified 
districts, so as to (a) bridge critical gap in loca l infrastructure and other 
development requirements that are not being adequately met through existiang 
inflows, (b) strengthen Panchayat and Municipality level governance with more 
appropriate capacity building, to facilitate participatory planning, decision making, 
implementation and monitoring, to reflect local felt needs, (c) provide professional 
support to local bodies for planning, implementation and monitoring their plans, 
(d) improve the performance and delivery of critica l functions assigned to 
Panchayats, and counter possible efficiency and equ ity losses on account of 
inadequate local capacity. 
The implementing Ministry for the BRGF districts is the Ministry of Panchayati Raj. 
The Ministry has prepared and issued the guidelines for implementation of the BRGF 
recently. The guidelines have been placed on the we bsite of the Ministry of 
Panchayati Raj (http://www.panchayat.gov.in).  The salient features of the guidelines 
issued by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj are as follows: 
(i) The BRGF covers 250 districts including all the  147 districts 
covered by the Rashtriya Sam Vikas Yojana (RSVY). 
(ii) BRGF consists of two funding windows, namely, a Capacity Building Fund 
of Rs. 250crore per annum, and a substantially untied grant. 
(iii) The substantially untied grant will be distri buted among the 
districts as follows: 
143 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2007] 
(a) every district will receive a fixed minimum amount of Rs. 10 crore 
per annum, and (b) the balance allocation under the scheme will be made 
on the basis of the share of the population and area of the districts in the 
total population and area of all the backward districts. 
  (iv) All the 147 RSVY districts will be released funds till the plans 
approved under RSVY (plus the existing monitoring f ee) have 
 been completed to the extent approved. Non RSVY—BR GF 
districts will begin the process of District Plan p reparation in  
2006-07 in accordance with these guidelines. 
(v) Each Panchayat or Municipality within the backw ard district 
concerned will be the unit for planning under BRGF.  Plans 
prepared by each Panchayat or Municipality will be consolidated into 
the District Plan by the District Planning Committe e, constituted in 
accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. 
(vi) During the consolidation of the District Plan, particular care shall be 
taken to ensure that the District Plan addresses issues relating to SC/ST 
development. 
(vii) The State Government will designate a departm ent, preferably the 
Department of Panchayati Raj, as the nodal departme nt at the State 
level, responsible for the management, monitoring and evaluation of 
the programme. 
(viii) A High Powered Committee headed by the State Chief Secretary and 
consisting of members from various departments of State Government 
and the Central Ministries will consider and approv e the proposed 
District Plans to be taken up under the districts c omponent of the 
BRGF. 
(ix) All funds will be transferred to the consolida ted funds of the State 
Governments. Those funds that are to be transferred  to Panchayats 
and Municipalities by the State Governments will be  transferred to 
their bank accounts within 15 days of the release o f funds to the 
Consolidated Funds. 
(x) Audit, Inspection of works, preparation of booklet of verification of 
works and progress reports will be done as per the procedure 
prescribed. 
(xi) Separate guidelines have been provided in Chapter 5 for the States and 
districts not covered by Park IX and Part IXA of the Constitution.

3.3 Provision of Training: 
The objectives of the training component of Capabil ity building 
(Component 'd' in Table 1 above) are as follows: 
(a) Upgrading the knowledge and skills of all Panchayat s and 
Municipalities elected representatives to better pe rform their 
responsibilities. 
(b) Orient key officials associated with functions devo lved to Panchayats 
and who are working under or closely with them to e ffectively serve 
and facilitate the Panchayats in the performance of devolved functions. 
(c) Improve functioning of the Gram Sabha, particularly  through building 
the capability of pressure groups such as SHGs and CBOs to participate 
more meaningfully. 
Within the broad parameters of the National Capability Building Framework 
prepared by the Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj (A nnexe-3), State and 
District specific training strategies and plans sho uld be prepared by 
respective State Governments, which will be suitably supported by the

years, addressing the components described above may be prepared by each State. 
For this purpose, States may designate a nodal agen cy, such as the SIRD for 
preparation and management of the training plan. Technical assistance may be 
provided by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj for the preparation of State 
specific perspective plan document for training. 
The High-level monitoring and implementation committee at the State level 
may approve the plan before implementation. The costs can include both capital 
and revenue costs. 
Funds will be released annually by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj on the 
following conditions: 
(a) Receipt of the plan approved by the High level committee set up at the

(b) Indication of the funds proposed to be retained at the State level for

programmes to be taken up in the year in question, with allocations for 
each component within it.

Gram Panchayat:

particularly in the approach to providing staff to the Gram Panchayat. Action 
may be taken by Panchayats on the following lines: 
(a) A trained community level person for agriculture extension: 
This individual will be a multi-tasked functionary to provide knowledge 
inputs to the community on agriculture, water manag ement, livestock 
development, post-harvest management and agri-busin ess. Selection could be 
done by the local PRI. 
(b) A gender empowerment community leader or volunteer: 
This individual will act as a coordinator in the vi llage and undertake 
activities for female literacy and micro finance. A n elected woman panchayat 
representative could also be chosen as a gender coo rdinator. This coordinator 
will facilitate women at the panchayat level to organize themselves into SHGs, 
encourage them to register with Panchayats in

3899. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the PRI ME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are making any efforts to manage the population to 
achieve good growth rate by utilizing the resources effectively; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
168 

[10 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the steps to be taken by Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The Government 
recognises the importance of managing the population to achieve good growth 
rate by effectively utilizing available resources and improve the quality of lives 
of people. Stabilizing population is important for promoting sustaniable 
development with more equitable distribution. Howev er, managing and 
stabilization of population is a function of making child and reproductive health 
care accessible and affordable for all, increasing the provision and outreach of 
primary and secondary education and removing gender  bias, extending basic 
amenities including sanitation, safe drinking water  and housing, besides 
empowering women and enhancing their employment opportunities. 
The National Population Policy, 2000 (NPP 2000) pro vides a policy 
framework for advancing goals and prioritizing stra tegies to meet the 
reproductive and child health needs of the people, and to achieve net 
replacement levels (Total Fertility Rate, TFR) by 2 010. The immediate 
objective of NPP 2000 is to address the unmet needs  for contraception, health 
care infrastructure and health personnel, and to provide integrated service delivery 
for basic reproductive and child health care. The medium-term objective is to bring 
the TFR to replacement levels by 2610, through vigorous implementation of inter-
sectoral operational strategies The long* term obje ctive is to achieve a stable 
population by 2045, at a level consistent with the requirements of sustainable 
economic growth, social development, and environmental protection. 
Recognizing the importance of health for social and  economic 
development and for improving the quality of life, the Government of India 
launched the National Rural Health Missi6n (NRHM) i n 2005. Provision of 
accessible, affordable, accountable, effective and reliable primary health care 
facilities especially to the poor and vulnerable se ctions of the population, 
bridging the gap in rural health care services thro ugh creation of a cadre of 
Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA), improved hospital care, decentralized 
planning, intersectoral convergence, maintaining gender balance and ensuring 
population stabilization constitute the basic features of the NRHM. The NRHM 
also includes the second phase of Reproductive and Child Health Programme, 
which intends to improve the performance of family welfare for reducing 
maternal and infant morbidity and mortality, 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2007] 
and unwanted pregnancies. These initiatives are lik ely to provide the right 
impetus for improving the health & family welfare s ervices, and hasten 
process of population stabilization in the country. 
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), which is a national flagship programme of the 
Government of India, is the vehicle for operationalising the strategy for universal 
elementary education in the country. The programme seeks to open new schools 
in uncovered habitations, augment school infrastruc ture through provision of 
additional classrooms, toilets, drinking water, etc . The aim is to provide 
elementary education to all children in the 6-14 years age-group by 2010.

Protection to Indian sailors under Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 
3912.  DR. ABISHEK MANU SINGHVI: 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
182 

[10 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 enables Gov ernment to 
impound a ship registered in a foreign country, whe n there is a death due to 
negligence or murder of Indian sailors on such ships; 
(b) if so, the manner in which Government assures that our sailors get due 
justice whenever any serious physical injury or death comes to their notice suo 
moto or is specifically brought to their notice; and 
(c) whether the provisions of this Act of 1958 are adeq uate to protect 
interests of Indian sailors or whether any amendment is required? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS 
(SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) Any accident including the d eath or injury to any 
seafarer of any nationality on board a ship registe red in foreign country while 
the said vessel is on or near the coast of India ca n be invested by an officer 
appointed under section 359 of the Merchant Shippin g Act, 1958. During the 
course of investigation, the vessel or its crew can be detained for the purpose of 
conducting the investigation. However, if the death is due to any criminal act 
such as murder, the relevant provisions of the Indi an Panal Code/Criminal 
Penal code would apply and the Merchant Shipping Ac t, 1958 does not have 
any provisions to address such issues. 
(b) In cases where an Indian seafarer gets injured and dies on a foreign 
registered ship while the vessel is at high seas, i t is the jurisdiction of the 
respective flag administration to conduct investiga tion into the cause of such 
accident or criminal incident. The Government of In dia, being a substantially 
interested state, however, has now also started participating as observer in such 
investigation wherever possible. Further, whenever feasible, the Indian 
Embassy/High Commission officials are intimated to investigate the matter in 
the first port of call in the foreign countries. 
(c) The Indian Merchant Shipping Act address the subjec t of protecting 
interests of Indian sailors in various sections. However, to further strengthen the 
existing provisions following additional measures h ave been initiated by the 
Directorate General of Shipping. 
(i) Recruitment and Placement Rules, 2005 have been  notified to 
regulate various manning agents who employ Indian Seasfarers. This 
notification requires mandatory registration of such manning agents 
operating out of offices registered in India. This has ensured that 
manning agents, who employ Indian seasfarers on 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2007] 
Indian as well as foreign registered vessels, are held accountable to the 
welfare of such Indian seafarers. 
(ii) A psychometric test has been introduced at the  entry level of 
officers in maritime training courses, which will help in determining 
his/her attitude and aptitude for the sea. It assis ts in taking 
corrective measures to mentally prepare for rigours of a life at sea. 
(iii) The Directorate General of Shipping has also made wide publicity in 
leading newspapers with regard to the recruitment t hrough the 
registered Recruitment and Placement Shipping Agent s for 
employment in marine sector. 
(iv) A new course module has been formulated to sen sitize the trainees 
with regard to rights of seafarers as laid down und er the Merchant 
Shipping (Recruitment and Placement) Rules, 2005 in  all Pre-sea 
Training Institutes. 
(v) The matter has also been taken up with the Inte rnational Maritime 
Organization (IMO) with regard to consolidating the  international 
conventions with regard to shipping casualty and ma king the law 
stringent to bring around the non-responsible flat state to carry out 
their responsibility. 
(vi) MS Notice No. 5-A has been issued by the D.G.S . This notice 
requires mandatory reporting and plan of action to deal with 
casualities involving Indian seafarers on foreign flat ships.

TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (SHRI K.H. MUNIAPPA): (a) an d (b)

the Government) on perpetuity is collected by the Government.

cost of the construction and the expenditure on ann ual maintenance for the

209

cost of the construction and the expenditure on ann ual maintenance for the 
concession period. The cost of project is recovered  through Annuity payment 
(semi annually). However, the toll revenue is collected by the Government. 
(d) BOT (Toll) mode is advantageous to Government as the risk of traffic growth 
and recovery of revenue lies on the private entrepreneur who raises fund to build 
and operate the projects and therefore, lower Gover nment funding is required 
to implement it.

MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFIC E 
(SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. ISR O is planning to 
launch an advanced dedicated meteorological satelli te INSAT-3D with 6 
channel high-resolution imager and 19 channel atmospheric sounder to provide 
temperature and humidity profiles, hitherto not available over our region for the 
meteorological community. Further, the launching of Indian Remote Sensing 
satellites, namely, Oceansat-2 with advanced Scatte rometer for ocean surface

systems, India will have a space-based synoptic obs erving capability for 
monitoring of weather related parameters such as cl oud structures, humidity, 
temperature and wind. While such advanced meteorolo gical satellites help to 
provide enhanced observational capability for improved meteorological services, 
an optimum combination of data from different sourc es including in-situ 
information is important to prescribe the atmospher ic state with accuracy, 
reliability, frequency and coverage. Towards this, efforts are also being made to 
augment the ground-based system such as LIDAR, Dopp ler Weather Radars, 
Automatic Weather Stations and Agro-meteorological

towers. Assimilation of such vast amount of data into operational numerical weather 
prediction models is an important steps to improve the prediction of monsoons and 
aderse extreme weather events. Better understanding of the atmospheric processes 
will also help the disaster mitigation acivities fo r events such as cyclone, 
drought, and cloudbursts with timely early warning.

3962. SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS 
AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of schemes implemented by Sports Authority of India (SAI) 
for spotting and nurturing of sports talent, promotion of sports in the country; 
(b) the quantum of funds incurred on sports promotion during the last three 
years, sports-wise/year-wise; and 
(c) the details of achievement made in international sp orts during the last 
three years? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI  
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) The details of schemes implemen ted by the Sports 
Authority of India (SAI) for spotting and nurturing  sports talent and the 
promotion of sports in the country are under:— 
NATIONAL SPORTS TALENT CONTEST (NSTC): The main objective of 
the scheme is to scout talent among school children  in the age of 8—14 years 
and nurture them by imparting scientific training i n SAI-adopted schools and 
'akharas' to achieve excellence at national and int ernational levels. SAI also 
provides coaches and special infrastructure facilit ies to these schools and 
akharas along with annual grant for purchase of sports equipments. 
237 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2007] 
ARMY BOYS SPORTS COMPANIES (ABSC): The objective of  the 
scheme is to scout talent in the age group of 8-14 years in collaboration with the 
Army and impart of them scientific training in thei r Centres to achieve 
excellence at national and international levels. Th e scheme, inter alia, also 
provides job opportunities in the Indian army. 
SPECIAL AREA GAMES (SAG): The objective of the sche me is to scout 
and nurture talent for modern competitive games and  sports from tribal, rural, 
coastal and hilly areas of the country and from regions such in sports talent, in 
terms of genetic and geographical characteristics/ advantages for excellence in 
particular sports disciplines. 
The main objective of the scheme is to train talented and meritorious sports 
persons in the age group of 14-21 years. Under the Scheme, the State 
Governments are required to provide land free of co st to SAI, while the 
development of the infrastructure is done by SAI. 
SAI TRAINING CENTRES(STC): Under this schemes, talented youth in the 
age group of 14-21 years are selected after assessment based on performance at 
national/state level competions and through a batte ry of tests. The selected 
trainees are given the option to join the scheme on residential or non-residential 
basis. The scheme is directly implemented by SAI. H owever, the state 
Government is required to provide the land and necessary sports infrastructure and 
other allied facilities like hostel building, etc. to the SAI. 
CENTRES OF EXCELLENCE (COX): The main objective of this scheme is to 
identify and train outstanding sports persons who a re medal hopes for the 
country in international competitions. The scheme o f Centre of Excellence 
envisages identification of talent in the country w ho has shown promising 
performance in the national competitions for furthe r training at the Regional 
Centres of SAI for nearly 200 days in a year. They are provided with state-of-art 
facilities, equipment and scientific backup alongwith specialized training. 
In all these schemes there is provision for payment  of stipend and 
medical/insurance expenses, kit and competition exposure.

India's unsuccessful bid to host Asian Games 2014 
3965. SHRI T.T.V DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS 
AND SPORTS be pleased to State: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India unsuccessfully trie d to host Asian Games 
in New Delhi in 2014; and 
(b) if so, the reasons for failure? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI  
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) It would appear from the outcome that the prese ntation made by the 
Republic of Korea carried more weight with the Electoral College than the Indian 
presentation partly because the RoK delegation said they would be showcasing all 
of Asia at Incheon, and not just RoK alone, and because they argued that such 
Games are awarded to cities not countries and Delhi had earlier been the venue 
of two Asian Games, in 1951 and 1982 respectively, whereas Incheon had not 
earlier hosted the Games. As the ballot was secret and no explanation of vote was 
required either before or after the vote, it is not possible to categorically state the 
reasons for which the vote was lost but it is to be  noted that the Chairman of 
the Olympic Council for Asia announced that the vote was decided by "a narrow 
margin".

3966. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS AND 
SPORTS be pleased to state:. 
(a) the causes for the utter poor performance of our Indian cricket team during 
the recent world cup series; 
(b) the persons who are responsible for this disastrous defeat; 
(c) the corrective measures taken in this regard; and 
(d) whether they would be effective and adequate? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI  
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) The Board of Control fo r Cricket in India 
(BCCI), which is the recognized National Sports Fed eration for this sports 
discipline, has informed Government that it is of the view that the Indian 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2007] 
Team did not perform to its full potential and one bad game against Bangladesh was 
responsible for the early exit of Indian Team from the World Cup-2007. The BCCI holds 
the poor performance to be the collective responsibility of the whole team. 
(c) and (d) To ensure better performance of the Indian Cricket Team, the Board of Control 
for Cricket in India had organized a brainstorming session at which former cricket captains 
were invited and, in consequence, several measures have been taken which include intensive 
training inputs in different aspects of the game; norms in terms of minimum level of 
participation in domestic competitions; encouraging young potential players, etc.

Effect of Earthquake  
*541. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of EARTH 
SCIENCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Northern India was rocked be earthquake 
recently; 
  (b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have identified earthquake prone areas in the 
country; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
8 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) whether the local administration of these areas has been advised about 
the type of construction to be carried out in these areas to withstand the effect of 
earthquakes; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) The following two significant earthquakes have been experienced 
in the northern parts of India in the recent past: 
(1) An earthquake of magnitude 7.6 occurred on 8th October, 2005 at 09 
Hours 21 Minutes IST with its epicenter at latitude  34.5 degree 
North and longitude 73.2 degree East in Pakistan. The earthquake had 
caused extensive damage to property and loss of life in Jammu and 
Kashmir. The earthquake was also widely felt in other northern parts 
of the country including Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, 
Uttar Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Rajasthan and Delhi. Th e main shock 
was followed by several aftershocks of lower intens ities with 
decreasing frequency. 
(2) An earthquake of magnitude 5.9 with its epicenter a t latitude 36.9 
degree North and 70.6 degree East longitude in Hindukush-Afghanistan 
region occurred at 09 Hours 05 Minutes IST on 3rd A pril, 2007. 
The earthquake was reported widely felt in northern  parts of 
India including Delhi. 
 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) Bureau of Indian Standards [IS-1893 (Part-I): 2002], based on various 
scientific inputs from a number of agencies, has grouped the country into four 
seismic zones viz. Zone-ll, III, IV and V as shown in Statement-I (See below). Of 
these, Zone V is the most seismically active region, while zone II is the least. The 
Modified Mercalli (MM) intensity, which measures the impact of the earthquakes 
on the surface of the earth Statement-ll (See below ), broadly associated with 
various zones is as follows:  
Seismic Zone Intensity on MM scale 
II (Low intensity zone) , 
III (Moderate intensity zone) 
IV (Severe intensity zone) 
V (Very severe intensity zone) 
VI (or less) 
VII 
VIII 
IX (and above)

RAJYA SABHA  [14 May, 2007] 
Broadlly, Zone-V comprises of the entire northeaste rn India, parts of 
Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttaranchal, R ann of Kutch in 
Gujarat, parts of North Bihar and Andaman & Nicobar islands. Zone-IV covers 
remaining parts of Jammu & Kashmir and Himachal Pra desh, Union 
Territory of Delhi, Sikkim, northern parts of Uttar  Pradesh, Bihar and West 
Bengal, parts of Gujarat and small portions of Maha rashtra near the west 
coast and Rajasthan. Zone-Ill comprises of Kerala, Goa, Lakshadweep islands, 
remaining parts of Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and West Bengal, parts of Punjab, 
Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar Jharkhand, Chhatti sgarh, Maharashtra, 
Orissa, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. Zone-ll covers remaining 
parts of the country. 
(e) and (f) The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) ha s brought out 
several publications useful for construction practi ces in the country, which 
are required to be adopted for construction in eart hquake prone areas. In 
addition, National Building Code of India (2005), has also been brought out by 
BIS, which incorporates latest provision of relevant codes related to design and 
construction of earthquake resistant buildings. The  above-referred standards 
cover different types of construction and cater to the requirements of various 
parts of the country. Ministry of Housing and Urban  Poverty Alleviation has 
been advising State Governments for adopting disast er resistant construction 
technologies in the housing projects. 
To ensure construction of earthquake resistant hous es by strengthening 
techno-legal regime of respective States and UTs, a Model Town and Country 
Planning Legislation, Zoning Regulation Development Control and Building 
Regulation/Bye-laws for Safety against Natural Haza rds have been prepared 
by an Expert Committee constituted by the Ministry of Home Affairs. To help 
State Governments in amending their Acts/Bye-laws/R egulation, Building 
Materials and Technology Promotion council (BMTPC) has been organizing 
one-day Technical Workshops on Model Amendments in Town and Country 
Planning Act, zoning Regulation, Development and Co ntrol Regulation and 
Building Regulation for safety against natural haza rds in States/UTs to 
disseminate the recommendations of the Committee. T echnical Workshops 
have been organized in all 8 North-eastern States. In addition, Technical 
Workshops have also been organized in Tamil Nadu, C hhattisgarh, Bihar, 
Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Pondicherry and Andaman and Nicobar.

laws of the market, and the distribution sector is still reeling under losses, the 
private players are reluctant to invest money; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take to prom ote the private 
participation in power sector? 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) 
Out of the total installed capacity of 1,32,329 MW as on 31st March, 2007, 
the installed capacity in the private sector was 17 ,112 MW which is 12.9 per 
cent of the total installed capacity. 
(b) The decade of the 1990s saw the gradual deterioration of the financial health of 
State Electricity Boards (SEBs). As a result, the Independent Power Producers (IPPs) 
which were required as per the then existing laws to sell their power solely to the 
host State Electricity Board, found it increasingly difficult to get financial closure 
in view of poor payment security. 
The Government of India has notified the Electricit y Act, 2003 which 
creates a liberal framework for the development of the power sector through a 
variety of initiatives like unbundling of vertically integrated power utilities, de-
licensing generation, allowing open access in transmission, recognizing power 
trading as a distinct licensed activity, setting up  of Regulatory Commissions 
and requiring the commissions to fix tariffs in a m anner so as to ensure 
financial viability of power utilities, etc. 
In order to ensure that the tariff for sale of elec tricity is determined 
competitively, the Tariff Policy was notified by th e Central Government in 
January, 2006, which provides that "all future requirement of power should be 
procured competitively by distribution licensees ex cept in cases of expansion 
of existing projects or where there is a State cont rolled/owned company as an 
identified developer and where regulators will need  to resort to tariff 
determination based on norms provided that expansion of generating capacity 
by private developers for this purpose would be restricted to one time addition of 
not more than 50% of the existing capacity. Even for the Public Sector projects, 
tariff of all new generation and transmission proje cts should be decided on 
the basis of competitive bidding after a period of five years or when the 
Regulatory Commission is satisfied that the situation is ripe to introduce such 
competition". 
Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides th at "the Appropriate 
Commission shall adopt the tariff if such tariff ha s been determined through 
transparent process of bidding in accordance with the guidelines issued by the 
Central Government". 
The restoration of the financial health of the State Electricity Boards/ State 
Utilities was recognized as the most critical challenge facing the sector. 
14 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
In this context, the distribution sector needed urgent attention to reverse the trend of 
deteriorating financial health of the sector. The reversal was sought to be addressed 
through a combination of the following key measures:— 
(i) control of theft of electricity. 
(ii) Reduction in the cost of supply through reduct ion in technical 
losses. 
(iii) Better management and lowering the cost of generation. 
(iv) Payment of user charge and Tariff rationalization. 
Further, the Government of India launched the Accel erated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) in 2002-0 3 aimed at 
effecting reduction in distribution losses under wh ich additional central 
assistance is being provided to the States for taki ng up various measures for 
reducing distribution losses. There have been improvements in billing, collection 
efficiency and the national average Aggregate Techn ical & Commercial 
(AT&C) losses of the distribution companies which h ave reduced from 
36.63% in 2002-03 to 34.54% in 2005-06. 
Encouraged by the Electricity Act, 2003 and other m easures, the 
Financial Institutions have agreed to consider fina ncial security arrangements 
other than Government guarantees. They have indicated availability of sufficient 
funds for good projects with viable tariff sponsored by credible promoters. 
(c) In addition to the above sector level initiatives, the Government have 
taken the following steps to promote private participation in power sector:— 
(i) One hundred per cent (100%) Foreign Direct Investment has been 
permitted on the automatic approval route in respec t of projects 
relating to electricity generation, transmission an d distribution 
(other than nuclear power plants). Recently, power trading has also 
been included in the above, subject to compliance w ith the 
regulations under the Electricity Act, 2003. 
(ii) Recognizing that cheaper power can be secured by reaping the 
benefits of economies of scale through development of large size 
power projects, the Government has taken an 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
initiative for facilitating the development of a fe w Ultra Mega 
Power Projects of about 4000 MW capacity each under  the tariff 
based competitive bidding route using cost effective super critical 
technology. 
(iii) The Government of India has been assisting wherever required, to 
resolve issues coming in the way of implementation of IPPs, 
including setting up of an Inter-Institutional Grou p (IIG) 
comprising of senior representatives from the Finan cial 
Institutions and Ministry of Power to facilitate ea rly financial 
closure of power projects. 
Encouraged by the enabling legislative framework an d the above 
initiatives, 16 private sector power projects aggre gating to capacity of 7320 
MW have achieved financial closure over last two years and have commenced 
construction.

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPlL SIBAL): (a) 
Yes, Sir. India Meteorological Department, based on the new statistical model 
predicted that the 2007 southwest seasonal (June to September) rainfall over the 
country is likely to be 5 per cent less than the long period average (LPA) (LPA:89 
cm based on 1941-1990.data). This forecast was made based on the data up to 
March, 2007. 
(b) Yes, Sir. It is true that several international meteorological institutes in US, 
UK and Europe have predicted above-average monsoon over India for the 2007 
southwest monsoon season. 
(c) and (d) These institutes prepare forecasts based on  coupled ocean-
atmosphere dynamical models, using initial data of April. They also take into 
account the EL-nino La Nina conditions. The dynamical models have reached the 
accuracy level of prediction of 7 days and research  work is going on to 
increase it to 10 days in nothern latitudes. Howeve r, the dynamical models do 
not give accurate forecasts in long term. However, some scientists in these 
institutes are trying to see whether the dynamical model will give reasonable 
accuracy due to averaging effects. This will take m any years to prove or 
disprove. 
IMD forecast is based on statistical method. A new method has been 
developed this year which gives in improved accuracy. IMD has more confidence in its 
synoptic and statistical methods for long range forecast than forecasts from these 
institutes that have stared these forecasts only recently. 
IMD will be issuing an updated forecast in June based on observation data up 
to May, 2007. More information on the evolution of sea surface temperature 
(SST) conditions (La Nina conditions) over the Pacific Ocean will be known by 
them.

4123. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of EARTH 
SCIENCES 
be pleased to state:

and nitrous oxide as a result of human activities s ince 1750 and increase in

socio-economic information relevant for the underst anding of climate 
change, its potential impacts and options for adapt ation and mitigation. The 
Report on this aspect is an assessment based on the  published scientific 
literature worldwide. It is synthesized by the expe rts in the relevant field 
under the aegis of the IPCC.

National Institute of Open Schooling gives the SCI ST students concession in 
admission fees to the extent of Rs. 200/- for bridg e courses, Rs. 250/- for 
secondary courses and Rs.300/- for senior secondary courses.

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
(a) to (d) In pursuance of the judgement of the Supreme Court of October 6.1993 
in the Supreme Court Advocates on Record & Anrs. vs. the Union of India the 
judge strength of the High Courts is reviewed every three years. 
1. 1  As per the guidelines, the required strength of permanent Judges in 
a High Court is worked out by dividing the average institution of main cases 
during the last five years by the national average or the average rate of disposal 
of main cases per Judge per year in that High Court, whichever is higher. 
1.2 Similarly, the required strength of Additional Judges in a High Court 
is worked out by dividing the number of main cases pending over two years by 
the national average or the average rate of disposal of main cases per Judge per 
year in that High Court, whichever is higher 
1.3 If the disposal per Judge in the concerned High Court is below even 
the national average then instead of increasing the  strength, the concerned 
High Court is required to take steps for improvement in the rate of disposal of 
cases. If the average disposal of concerned High co urt is above the national 
average then increase in Judge strength is accordingly considered. The strength of 
Additional Judges is reviewed only if there is an i ncrease in the arrears of the 
pending cases during the last 5 years and the dispo sal per Judge is above the 
national average.

(a) whether in view of more than 5,31,477 cases pending in High Courts for 10

(b) whether the Judges population ratio in India is 10.5 judges per million

judge-strength five-fold from 10.5 to atleast 50 judges per million?

99 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) 
Judicial Reforms is a continuous process and is a combined responsibility of all 
stakeholders including the Executive and the Judici ary. Both the Union 
Government and the State Governments continue their efforts including through providing 
financial support for carrying out and sustaining judicial reforms. The expenditure 
incurred by the High Courts including that for disposal of cases being charged on the 
Consolidated Fund of the State Governments, the States also have a major responsibility 
in this regard. In so far as the Union Government is concerned it is continuing its efforts 
for judicial reforms including that by providing fi nancial support to the State 
Governments by making budget provisions in this regard. Government approved a 
scheme for computerization of all District and subordinate courts of the country at 
a cost of Rs 442 crores. An amount of Rs.322.87 crore has been provided as Budger 
Estimates for 2007-08 for the Department of Justice for continuing both Plan and 
Non-Plan schemes aimed at efficient justice delivery. In addition to the Union 
Government's efforts, the States have also made appropriate provisions both for their 
respective High Courts and for its subordinate judiciary. 
(b) and (c) The 120th Law Commission in its Report of July, 1987 had 
mentioned that there was a justification for increasing the then ratio of 10.5 judges 
per million population to at least 50 million India n population. The Supreme 
Court, in its judgement of 21st March, 2002, in All  India Judges Association & 
Ors. Vs. Union of India & Ors. (all State Governments and Union Territories are 
also party to this case), directed that an increase in the Judge strength from the 
existing 10.5 or 13 per 10 lakh people to 50 judges per 10 lakh people would be 
effected and implemented within a period of five years in a phased manner to be 
determined and directed by the Union Ministry of Law. The Central Government 
have filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court praying that the increase in judge 
strength in the Union Territories for which Central Government is administratively 
responsible be allowed based on workload and pendency of cases. The matter is 
subjudice.

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) 
and (b) Under article 235 of the Constitution, administration of justice is a State 
subject and the State Government in consultation with its concerned High Court 
decides all matters concerning operations and setting up of courts. 
The matter of introduction of shift system in subordinate courts, among other 
things, was discussed in the Conference of Chief Mi nisters and Chief Justices 
of High Courts held in New Delhi on April 8, 2007. In that Conference all 
States had welcomed the introduction of shift system in subordinate courts and 
promised to work in that direction. It was decided in that Conference that 
evening/morning courts be set up, wherever found feasible, and appropriate cases 
including those involving petty offences be transfe rred to such courts. Either 
retired Judicial Officers be re-employed or serving  judicial Officers be given 
suitable incentive, to preside over these Courts. Government has requested the State 
Governments to take action on the above mentioned d ecision, as also on the 
other decisions of the Conference, in consultation with their respective High 
Courts. The Government has also requested that Chie f Justices of the High 
Courts to take action in consultation with the State Governments. 
(c) The Government has taken various steps/measures to improve the 
productivity and efficiency of the judiciary including periodically monitoring the 
pendency position in courts, grouping of cases involving common question of law, 
constitution of specialized benches, timely filling up the vacancies of judges, 
increasing the judge strength, organizing Lok Adala ts at regular intervals, 
encouraging alternative modes of disputes resolution like negotiation, mediation 
and arbitration and setting up of special tribunals  like Central Administrative 
Teibunals, State Administrative Tribunals, Income Tax Appellate Tribunals, Family 
Courts, Labour Courts, etc. The Government has also set up Fast Track Courts in 
States and has extended their term up to 31.03.2010 for clearing pending cases at 
District level. 
(d) and (e) The Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2006 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 23rd August, 2006, has among other things, a 
proposal to prevent the evil of witness turning hostile by amending sections 161, 
162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and als o by inserting new 
sections 164B and 344A in the Code to provide that

or more (iii) enhanced punishment for perjury.

Appointment of young judges  
4186. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any minimum age fixed for a person  to become a 
judge of any High Court; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what qualities does a person require to become a judge of a High Court; 
(d) whether it is a fact that some State Governments ha ve been 
recommending names of very young and untested people for appointments as 
judges in High Courts; and 
(e) whether Government will develop guidelines and conv entions to 
prevent nomination of very young people to High Courts? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): (a) 
to (e) The minimum age limit for appointment of a person as Judge of a High Court 
from the Bar is 45 years. However, the Chief Justices' Conference held in December. 
1999 unanimously resolved that members of the Bar over 40 years and less than 
45 years may be recommended for appointment as Judges of High Courts only if 
they possess outstanding merit, and rigidity that t he members of the Bar must 
be above 45 years of age for being appointed must n ot be insisted upon. For 
the members from the Judicial service, they should not have crossed the age of 
58-1/2 years on the date of availability of the vacancy for the service quota. 
104 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
As per the Constitution of India, a person should have practised for at least 
10 years before becoming a Judge of the High Court. Besides this, his academic 
attainments, standing and experience, specialisations, if any, competence in 
perception, ability to deal with complex legal prob lems, grasping capacity, 
Judicial Patential like maturity, temperament, capacity to persuade and to be 
persuaded, patience, fairness etc., Integrity and character and antecedents are kept in 
view while considering a person from the Bar. 
After the Supreme Court Judgment of October 6,1993 in the Supreme Court 
Advocates-on-Record and Anr. Vs. Union of India, read with their Advisory 
Opinion of October 28, 1998, the entire process of initiation of proposal for 
appointment of a Judge of the High Court lies with the Chief Justice of that 
High Court. While making recommendations, the Chief  Justices keep the 
above criterion in view.

SHRMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that out of one lakh deliverie s, 300 pregnant 
women die every year and with only an average of 16 point reduction in figure, 
India cannot reach its Millennium Development Goals of lowering the maternal 
deaths to 200 by 2007 and 109 by 2015; 
(b) whether this conclusion is based on the study repor t released by

would be required to meet the target; and 
209

(d) if so, the steps Government propose to achieve the target set up by

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) Based on the official estimates of Registrar 
General of India (RGI), emerging from the Sample Registration System conducted 
between 2001-2003 the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) for India is 301 per 
1,00,000 live births MMR for India and major states is given in the Statement (See 
below). As per the report released in October, 2006, by the office of Registar 
General of India, titled "Maternal Mortality in India: 1997—2003 Trends, Causes 
and Risk Factors" the overall average rate of MMR decline during the period 1997-
2003 has been 16 points per year. At this rate of decline, as per the projection given 
by RGI it is expected that MMR would be in the range of 195—230 per 1,00,000 
live births by the year 2012. 
The National Population Policy 2000 and National Health Policy 2002 have 
set the goal of reducing MMR to less than 100 per 100,000 live births by the year 
2010. The Government of India is already implementi ng programmes to 
achieve the goals of reduction in Maternal Mortality Ratio. Accordingly, schemes 
and programmes have been developed to provide basic  health facilities 
especially in rural areas including those at the time of delivery. 
Government of India has launched the National Rural  Health Mission 
(NRHM) in the year 2005, with special emphasis on improving the health status 
of rural population throughout the country. Under the NRHM (2005-2012) and 
Reproductive and Child Health Programme Phase-ll (R CH-II) with the above 
goal in view, the GOI is strengthening services by implementation of the 
following key interventions: 
• Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), a scheme to promote Institutional 
Delivery for reducing Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR ) and Infant 
Mortality Rate (IMR) by providing quality maternal care during 
pregnancy, delivery and immediate post-delivery per iod with 
appropriate referral transport system along with ca sh assistance to 
pregnant women with a special focus on Below Poverty Line (BPL) 
women. The scheme also covers SC/ST women delivering in the Govt. 
Health Institutions and accredited Private Institutions. 
. 2 1 0  
 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
• Appointment of an Accredited Social Health Activist  (ASHA) for 
every village with a population up to 1000. ASHA wi ll facilitate in 
accessing of health care services by the community and will have 
specific responsibility of mobilizing pregnant women for ante-natal 
care, institutional delivery and post-natal check u ps and 
immunization to children. 
• Ensuring skilled attendance at every birth both in the community and 
the Institutions. 
• Operationalizing Community Health Centers as First Referral Units 
(FRU) for providing Emergency Obstetric and Child Health Services. 
At present, as reported by the states 2153 FRUs are  being made 
operational. 
• Equipping 50% of Primary Health Centres for providi ng 24x7 
delivery services by 2010. At present, as reported by the states 6550 
PHCs are functioning for 24-hours delivery services  including 
new-born care. 
• Ensuring quality of services by implementing Indian Public Health 
Standards (IPHS) for Primary Healthcare Facilities,  which 
includes providing infrastructure, specialized man- power and 
equipments. 
• Training of MBBS Doctors in Life Saving Anesthetic Skills for 
Emergency Obstetric Care at First Referral Unit.

Study on impact of global warming  
*528 SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that towns and cities along India's eastern 
coast would be devastated with global warming intensifying cyclones and rising sea 
levels eroding vast stretches of the shorelines; 
(b) if so, whether Government have done any comprehensive study on the 
impact of global warming in the coastal areas; 
(c) if so, the details there of; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefore? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (d) The Government is 
aware of the implication of the sea level rise due to projected climate change. 
The past observations on the mean sea level along t he Indian coast show a 
long-term rising trend of about 1.0 mm/year. The recent data suggests a rising trend 
of 2.5 mm/year in the sea-level along Indian coastline. Model simulation studies, 
indicate that the oceanic region adjoining the Indi an subcontinent is likely to 
warm at its surface by about 1.5-2.0 degree Centigrade by the middle of this 
century and by about 2.3-3.5 degree Centigrade by t he end of the century. The 
corresponding thermal expansion, related sea-level rise is expected to be between 
15 cm and 38 cm by the middle of this century and between 46 cm and 59 cm 
by the end of the century. According to a study con ducted by the Ministry of 
Environment & Forests on the impacts of climate cha nge on various sectors 
including coastal zones, in the event of one meter sea-level rise, 5764 Km2 of 
land in coastal areas of India is projected to lose , displacing approximately 7.1 
million people along with 4200 Kms of roads by the end of the 21st century. Further 
the coastal areas are also vulnerable to projected increase in 
218 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
frequency and intensity of extreme weather events l ike storm surges and 
cyclones. In the eastern coast, the vulnerable dist ricts include Jagatsinghpur 
and Kendrapara in Orissa and Nellore in Andhra Pradesh and Nagapattinam in 
Tamil Nadu.

*531.   DR.ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI: 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the observations ma de by 
Pakistan's Minister for Environment, on the sidelin es of Delhi Sustainable 
Development Summit, 2007 held during 4th week of January, 2007, that "India 
should focus on the environmental aspects of Siache n Glaciers which are 
melting at a faster rate due to global warming and continuous hu man traffic 
owing to heavy development of troops; 
(b) if so, what is the reaction of Government keeping the security of the 
nation in view.towards the suggestion of Pakistan's Minister; and 
(c) whether a comparative study has been made of other similar glaciers 
regarding the magnitude of melting rate where there is no human traffic? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) Y es, Sir. 
However, as per the information made available by t he Geological Survey of 
India, the total retreat of Siachen Glacier during the last 95 years (1909-2004) is 
about 500 meters at an average annual rate of 5.3 meter per year only. Thus the 
observations made by the Pakistani Minister are not  based on the factual 
data.Moreover, no proposal has been received by the 
224 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Government of India from Government of Pakistan regarding environmental aspects 
of Siachen Glaciers, although media reports from Pa kistan occasionally refer 
to the environmental benefits of the demilitarisati on of the area. Also, in 
proportion to the vastness of the Siachen Glacier, the actual deployment of the 
troops is small, which can have negligible effect on its melting. 
(c) Geological Survey of India has also undertaken studies on recession 
of several Himalayan glaciers, including Siachen Glacier. These studies revealed 
that the majority of glaciers of Himalayan region are passing through a phase 
of recession, as has been the case with the glacier s located in other parts of 
the world. The rate of recession in Himalayan regio n in different climatic 
zones is found to be variable in different years. This variable rate of recession 
can be attributed to the several climatic factors.

million people will be living with cancer. 
The data collected by Indian Council of Medical Res earch through 
Population Based Cancer Registry functioning under the National Cancer Control 
Programme, reveals that about 7-9 lakhs new cancer cases are detected every 
year and at any given point of time there are 2.25 million 
230 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
cancer patients in the country. Tobacco is one of t he main causes of cancer 
including Oral Cancer. 
As per revised scheme of National Cancer Control Programme (NCCP), 
special emphasis is now being laid on early detecti on of cancer by promoting 
health education and creating awareness.Financial a ssistance is provided for 
setting up Radiotherapy unit in Government Medical Colleges/Hospitals for 
providing cancer treatment facilities. In addition,  comprehensive cancer 
detection testing facilities in respective regions/ States are provided by 25 
Regional Cancer Centres developed over the years un der NCCP. Financial 
assistance is also provided to persons below povert y line from Rashtriya 
Arogya Nidhi for treatment of cancer. During Eleven th Plan, special focus is 
made to expand District Cancer Control Programme fo r early detection and 
management of cancer and to create infrastructure b y upgrading existing 
RCC, creating more RCCs,setting up of cancer treatm ent centres across the 
country with a view to producing quality manpower and treatment facilities. 
Water borne diseases 
†*538. SHRI KESHUBHAI S. PATEL: Will the Minister o f HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the World Health Organisation has warned about 
increase in water borne diseases caused by mosquito es and also in the area 
affected by these diseases; 
(b) if so, whether Government have taken any step so far, for prevention of 
diseases; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) Cholera, viral hepatitis, enteric fever and 
acute diarrhoeal diseases are the main water borne diseases caused by 
contamination of water with virus and bacteria, whe reas diseases caused by 
mosquitoes which mainly breed in water are vector b orne diseases like 
dengue, malaria, filariasis, viral encephalitis etc. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [14 May, 2007] 
World Health Organization, while assessing the association between climate 
change and health has projected that under warmer c limate conditions, 
stagnant water and scarcity of water will increase chances of cholera outbreaks. 
Changes in temperature and moisture would also incr ease the morbidity and 
mortality of vector borne diseases like malaria, Ja panese encephalitis and 
dengue. 
Health is primarily a State subject and provision of medical relief for water 
borne and vector borne diseases through primary and community health centres 
is looked after by the State Governments. The preventive measures taken by the 
local health authorities include provision of safe drinking water, improvement 
of personal and community hygiene, safe disposal of  human excreta, 
undertaking appropriate health education, surveilla nce and monitoring, 
distribution of chlorine tablets and ORS packets etc. 
A comprehensive National Vector Borne Disease Contr ol Programme 
(NVBDCP) is implemented through the States for prevention and control of vector 
borne diseases caused by mosquitoes. The strategies for control of vector borne 
diseases include disease management through early c ase detection and 
treatment, epidemic preparedness and rapid response . Integrated vetor 
management includes residual spraying, use of insecticide treated bed nets and anti 
larval measures. 
The Government of India supplements the efforts of the State 
Governments/Union Territories by providing funds under the Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme, Accelerated Urban Water Sup ply Programme, 
Total Sanitation Campaign, School Sanitation and Hygiene Education and Low 
Cost Sanitation Scheme for tackling quality related  problems in respect of 
rural and urban drinking water supply. National Ins titute of Communicable 
Diseases, Delhi (NICD) provides technical support t o the State Governments 
and undertake surveillance, early detection and pre vention and control of 
outbreaks of communicable diseases. 
An integrated approach has been initiated with Department of Drinking Water 
Supply to provide the technical support to monitor the quality of drinking 
water in different States so as to prevent occurrence of water borne diseases. 
232 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
The Government of India has also launched an Integr ated disease 
Surveillance Programme in November, 2004, to furthe r strengthen 
identification of outbreaks of various diseases including water borne and vector 
borne diseases so that early intervention could be made and occurrence, 
disability and death due to such diseases could be reduced.

(i) an Inter-Ministerial Empowered Committee has be en set up to

(ii) Indian entrepreneurs are being issued with Letters of Permission for

Welfare policy for drought hit States  
†3976. DR. PRABHA THAKUR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any welfare policy for farmers to bail 
out farmers and agricultural labourers of drought h it States from their plight; 
and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The prime responsibility for taking 
immediate measures in the wake of natural calamities including drought is that 
of the State Governments concerned. Most of the State Governments have Relief 
Code or Scarcity Manual to specifically deal with d roughts or for handling 
natural calamities including drought. The Government of India supplements the 
efforts* of the States with financial and logistic support, in accordance with the 
recommendations of the Finance Commissions for droughts and other natural 
calamities . Ready availability of funds exists with the States in the Calamity 
Relief Fund (CRF) for taking immediate measures in the wake of natural 
calamities including drought.

community including the landless.

which aims at generation of employment in the rural  areas for integrated and 
sustainable development of land and equitable shari ng of the benefits. The 
project envisages development of wastelands/ degrad ed lands based on 
village/micro watershed plans. The IWDP projects ar e prioritized for

has also recommended that the Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) should respond speedily 
to exigencies, specially in the case of sensitive c rops in the rainfed areas. The 
recommendations of the National Commission on Farmers have been examined in 
consultation with the subject matter. Ministries and State Governments and a note has 
been circulated for the consideration of the Committee of Secretaries. A final decision on 
the recommendations of the Commission has not been taken by the Government 
so far. 
However, the Government is implementing a Price Support Scheme (PSS) for 
procurement of oilseeds and pulses through NAFED and a Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) 
for procurement of perishable agricultural and horticultural commodities not covered under 
PSS, in order to protect the growers from making distress sales.

representatives from stakeholder Ministries. The Ex ecutive Committee is

(b) whether it is also a fact that the percentage of those rural households who are 
not having enough food everyday in some months is highest in West Bengal, 10.6 per cent, 
followed by Orissa, 4.8 per cent and Assam 3.6 per cent; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take to ensure that all people in the 
country get enough food daily ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION ( DR. AKHILESH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) No, Sir. On the basis of the results of National Sample Survey (NSS) 
61st Round (2004-05), survey data on household consumer expenditure Report No. 
512(61/1.0/5) conducted by National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), it is seen 
that, in rural as well as urban areas members of households getting enough food 
throughout the year has increased. Also, the number  of households in which 
members were not getting enough food has decreased. 
(b) In the Report conducted by National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), it has 
been estimated that the percentage of households not getting enough food every day in 
any month of the year is 1.3% in West Bengal, 1.3% in Orissa and 0,6% in Assam. 
(c) For ensuring food security particularly to the poor citizens, the Targeted Public 
Distribution System (TPDS) is being operated. The TPDS is primarily focused to cover the 
Below Poverty Line (BPL) families. The poorest of the poor among them are covered 
specifically under the Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY). Foodgrains are being distributed at 
highly subsidized prices to BPL and AAY poor families all over the country under the TPDS 
@ 35 kg per household per month. Foodgrains are also being distributed to States and Union 
Territories for different sections of societies under several welfare schemes. 
In addition to above the open market also takes care of the food needs of citizens. 
The Government keeps a continuous watch on the food situation and whenever there arise 
situations of shortage, the Government intervenes to import food items and makes them 
available in the market to augment supplies.

(a) to (c) No such complaints regarding sale of imported food stuffs after lapse 
of their expiry period date has come to the notice of the Department of Consumer 
Affairs. This subject comes within the purview of t he Prevention of Food 
Adulteration Act; 1954 and the Rules framed thereun der, administered by the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Implementation of the said Act and Rules 
are entrusted with the Food (Health) Authorities of the States/UTs. They have 
been instructed to lift samples of imported food articles sold in the market and

all edible/food products, domestic sale and manufacture of which are governed by 
prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 shall also be subject to the condition that 
at the time of importation, the products are having a valid shelf life of not less 
than 60 % of their original shelf life. Accordingly  all Port/Airport Health 
Officers and Custom Collectors at Ports/ Airports have been advised to ensure 
that all the imported food articles comply with all the above provisions before the 
same are released into the country for human consumption.

Hazardous Waste  
4036. SHRI C.PERUMAL: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that about 4.4 million tonnes of hazardous wastes are 
generated annually in our country; 
(b) if so, whether Government have analyzed the consequences; and 
(c) the details of action taken by Government to tackle  this problem of 
increasing environmental pollution in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) According to the 
report of the High Powered Committee on Hazardous wastes constituted by the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court and the assessment of waste g eneration carried out in 
accordance with the Hazardous Wastes (Management and Handling) amendment 
Rules, 2000, about 4.4 million tonnes of hazardous wastes are generated annually in 
our country. The improper handling and indiscriminate disposal of such wastes are 
likely to cause environmental pollution. 
(c) The Government of India has notified the Hazard ous Wastes 
(Management and Handling) Rules, 1989 under the Env ironment (Protection) 
Act, 1986, which were amended in 2000 and 2003. The se rules regulate the 
generation, collection, storage, treatment, disposa l, export and import of 
hazardous wastes. According to these rules, all haz ardous wastes are required 
to be treated and disposed of in specially designed secured landfills. These rules as 
amendd in 2003 provide for the development of a com mon hazardous waste 
Treatment Storage and Disposal Facility (TSDF) thro ugh joint-venture 
partnership. The Ministry of Environment and Forests provides financial assistance 
in the form of Central Government subsidy to the tu ne of Rs. 2.00 crores for 
setting up of such facilities provided a matching g rant is given by the State 
Government. 
The amendments to these rules in 2003, provide for channelization of 
repyclable wastes listed in Schedule 4 of the rules. A procedure for 
326 

[14 May, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
registration of the recyclers has been laid down un der Rule 19 of the 
Hazardous Wastes (Management and Handling) amendmen t Rules, 2003. 
According to these rules, all hazardous wastes recyclers are required to obtain 
consents under Water (Prevention and Control of Pol lution) Act, 1974 and Air 
(Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and authorization under the Hazardous 
Waste Rules. The units recycling hazardous wastes a re also required to have 
enviromentally sound technologies and adequate provisions for treatment and 
disposal of the subsequent wastes generated. 
The Central Pollution Control Board has published a number of Guidelines for safe 
handling and disposal of hazardous wastes and to provide guidance to the State 
Pollution Control Boards and Pollution Control Committees of the Union Territories 
and the industries for handling hazardous wastes.
